title: Chapter IV Roadmap
notes: Open by naming the organizing metaphor from the notebook: curves are tracked by ledgers. The assigned source span is printed pages 293-355 and PDF pages 308-370, while the teaching source is the chapter-04 notebook. Walk left to right through Riemann-Roch, Hurwitz, embeddings, elliptic curves, canonical models, and P3 geography.

title: Genus And Divisors
notes: Use the signed point ledger before formulas become dense. A divisor records deposits and debts at points, degree is the total balance, and linear equivalence says two ledgers differ by the divisor of a rational function. Genus is the persistent background invariant controlling how many sections these ledgers can buy.

title: Riemann-Roch Balance
notes: Point to the notebook figure as a numerical sanity check rather than a proof. The blue and red quantities move, but their difference is pinned by degree and genus. Emphasize the two inspection regions: negative degree, where effectivity disappears, and high degree, where the residual term vanishes and dimensions become linear.

title: Special Versus Nonspecial
notes: Translate specialness into the same ledger language. A divisor is special exactly when the residual ledger K-D still has sections. The canonical degree 2g-2 marks the size of the residual budget. Genus zero and one deserve separate memory hooks because their canonical degrees are negative and zero.

title: Hurwitz As Cover Accounting
notes: Introduce Hurwitz as the cover version of the same accounting habit. The target genus is multiplied by the cover degree, and every ramification point adds a defect term. The saved notebook rows all have residual zero, which is the useful classroom check: a wrong branch count breaks the genus equation immediately.

title: Tame, Wild, Inseparable
notes: Make the warning precise without turning it into a detour. The displayed Hurwitz formula is the clean separable story, and in tame ramification the correction is the visible e minus one contribution. Wild ramification adds more different, while inseparable maps such as Frobenius have vanishing differentials and require different handling.

title: Linear Systems Embed Curves
notes: Read very ampleness as three tests on a ledger of sections. Base-point freeness gives a morphism, separating points gives injectivity, and separating tangent directions gives an immersion. The picture lets students see why one missing test changes the projective model even when the degree looks large.

title: Every Curve Reaches P3
notes: Explain this as a projection theorem rather than magic compression. A sufficiently positive line bundle embeds the curve in a large projective space. A general projection down to P3 keeps the curve embedded when its center avoids the secant and tangent bad loci, so the curve becomes inspectable in three-dimensional projective space.

title: Plane Models With Nodes
notes: Use the node picture to separate arithmetic genus from geometric genus. A smooth plane curve of degree d has arithmetic genus (d-1)(d-2)/2. Each ordinary node identifies two branches and lowers the geometric genus by one, so the same abstract curve can be represented by a singular plane model.

title: Elliptic Curves From Branch Points
notes: Frame the elliptic classification through a four-point ledger on P1 in characteristic not two. Three branch points can be normalized to 0, 1, and infinity; the fourth is lambda, but lambda is only remembered up to the usual cross-ratio orbit. The j-formula packages that orbit into an isomorphism invariant.

title: A Cubic Becomes A Group
notes: Connect the notebook's exact residual check to the group law. A line meets a smooth cubic in three points counted with multiplicity, and the chosen origin turns collinearity into P plus Q plus R equals zero. The plotted example verifies the relevant points on the cubic, so the drawing is tied to algebra.

title: Pic0 And The Jacobian
notes: Move from the chord picture to the functorial language. On a genus-one curve with base point P0, the map P to O(P-P0) identifies the curve with its degree-zero Picard group. For higher genus, Pic0 becomes the Jacobian, a group variety that records divisor classes rather than individual points.

title: Complex Uniformization Snapshot
notes: Keep this slide as a recall snapshot, not a proof of analytic theory. Over the complex numbers, a lattice quotient C over Lambda is a torus, and Weierstrass functions place it on a cubic. The point is compatibility: the analytic group law and algebraic cubic group law describe the same elliptic curve.

title: Frobenius And Hasse Invariant
notes: Treat the Hasse invariant as a computable detector in positive characteristic. For a smooth plane cubic, take f to the p minus one power and read the coefficient of (xyz) to the p minus one. Nonzero means ordinary behavior; zero means supersingular behavior, so Frobenius leaves a visible algebraic trace.

title: Canonical Morphism
notes: Return to the canonical divisor as a projective machine. Its degree is 2g-2, and for genus at least two the complete canonical system maps the curve to projective space of dimension g minus one. The main split is nonhyperelliptic curves embedding versus hyperelliptic curves factoring through a double cover of P1.

title: Clifford's Bound
notes: Use Clifford's theorem as the restraint on overly optimistic linear systems. For a special divisor, the dimension of the complete linear system cannot exceed half its degree, aside from the known equality patterns. This is the bridge from Riemann-Roch counting to the degree-genus restrictions that appear in P3.

title: Degree-Genus Geography In P3
notes: Tie the static chart and the interactive lab together. The notebook artifact plots canonical degree and low-degree P3 examples, while the lab lets students inspect which family or obstruction labels each point. The important habit is to test a proposed pair against Castelnuovo and Halphen-style constraints before searching for equations.

title: Castelnuovo And Low-Degree Classification
notes: Close by returning to numerical ledgers. The Castelnuovo curve gives an upper envelope for nondegenerate curves in P3, and the notebook's d at most seven list supplies concrete families on and below it.
